Number 8, anchoring. I've always found anchoring bias to be 1 of the most interesting forms of Trader bias. The basic idea of anchoring bias is that when we are asked to guess or predict something we're biased toward the first reference point offered Outside of Finance. This is most commonly seen in negotiation. If we're told the price of a car is 12,000, anything below that feels cheap and anything above feels expensive. Even if we find out later that the car is only worth 10,000. Will still find ourselves anchored, on the initial price heaps of Search proves this, weirdly anchoring works even if the initial number is unrelated to the question at hand. A simple anchoring experiment which my son did for science. Fair once and it worked goes as follows subjects. First draw a random number from 1 to 100 out of a bag. Then they're asked to guess, for example, How many African countries are in the United Nations? Those that Drew low numbers from the bag answer consistently lower than those who drew higher numbers out of the bag. Another famous example of anchoring is when you ask people to quickly estimate 1 * 2, * 3, * 4, * 5, * 6, * 7 * 8. You get a much lower answer than if you asked them to quickly estimate. 8, * 7, * 6, * 5 * 4, * 3, * 2 * 1. In negotiation, you often hear never make the first offer because you're giving up too much information and optionality. in contrast and effective, negotiation strategy can be for 1 side to make an Outrageous, first offer there by anchoring the negotiation on a figure that's hard to get away from say, your negotiating with an employer, you want to get paid thousand dollars a year and you believe you have decent power in the negotiation. You open by suggesting a salary of 650,000. Now, both sides are anchored. So high that, when you finally settle on 550,000, everyone feels like a winner. Once you know about anchoring, you see it all over the place, especially in how companies price their goods treadmill was 1,299. Now 9.99, That sounds like a good deal but it could well be. The company has never sold a single unit for 1,299 and they're just trying to Anchor. You on that inflated price to make you feel good about paying 9.99. In markets anchoring bias, manifests in 4 main ways. 1, we anchor on our entry point. This is the most common and Powerful way you see anchoring by In markets, if you buy a stock at $99.40, that specific level becomes very powerful in your mind, you'll find it. Much easier for example to sell at 99.41 small profit than 99.39 a small loss, even though the economics of selling at these 2, different levels is practically identical. Losing is painful and negative winning is pleasurable and positive. So even though, 2 senses, meaningless to your pnl, the difference between selling below, or above your cost, is the difference between winning and losing, Human beings are hardwired to avoid losses as discussed earlier. Research shows the pain, we feel from losses is about double the pleasure we get from gains of equal size. This bias is called loss aversion. A related bias is the disposition effect. This is the strong and consistent tendency for investors to prefer to sell assets that have increased in value. While holding on to assets that show a If it goes up, you sell it. If it goes down, you hold on to it and pray for a bounce. These related forms of bias all come down to the same thing. Humans don't like to lose. The remedy is simple. You must learn to love small losses. When you take a small loss, try to feel good about it, say taking small losses is the way to achieve trading success. Say it over and over taking small losses, is the way to achieve trading, success taking small losses is the way to achieve trading, success, taking small losses is the way to achieve trading success. Trading losses are an expense incurred by your trading business. Your goal is to minimize trading loss expense while maximizing trading Revenue. You minimize trading loss expense by cutting bad trades quickly and by sticking to your plan, you increase trading loss expense with shoddy risk management, poor discipline and sloppy Trading. as a beginning Trader, you will no doubt hear your Yourself thinking this trade feels wrong as soon as I get to break, even I'm out. 2 problems here. Problem 1. This trade feels wrong, is not rational unpack. Why it feels wrong? Is there something inherently wrong with the price action? Or is the stock just not moving and you're bored? Those are 2 completely different things. Often your instincts are just your impatience and emotions trying to sabotage a perfectly good trade. Problem 2. As soon as I get to break, even I'm out is not logical. Do you think the market cares where you got in as if there's something magical about your entry point, if you've determined biologic that the trade is not worth holding on to get out. If you've not determined you should get out of the trade, maintain your existing parameters. Every trade you put on should have a stop loss and a take profit after that.
